The present contribution, however, attests evidence of a two-tone pitch contrast between high (H) and low (L) in monosyllabic and disyllabic nouns. All three pieces of the composite quote are present verbatim at the stated locators: printed p. 49 (= PDF p. 59), sec. 4 'Tone on Tagoi nouns': 'Stevenson instead claims that stress plays a marked role and may be responsible for grammatical and lexical contrast in Tagoi (Stevenson 1956/1957: 47; 1964: 86). The present contribution, however, attests evidence of a two-tone pitch contrast between high (H) and low (L) in monosyllabic and disyllabic nouns. Thus, it might be that Stevenson noticed the pitch distinction but he attributed it to stress.'; printed p. 43 (= PDF p. 53), sec. 1.2: 'data in the present contribution show evidence in favour of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tagoi is analysed as a two-tone (H/L) language: lexical minimal pairs on mono- and disyllabic nouns (e.g. cɔ́r 'orphan' vs cɔ̀r 'moon'), tone borne by every mora, no phonemic contour tones (phonetic HL fall on word-final long syllables). The earlier claim (Stevenson 1956-57: 47; 1964: 86, followed by Tucker & Bryan 1966) that Tagoi/Rashad has dynamic stress rather than tone is explicitly rejected as a misreading of the pitch contrast. No source seen states a position for word stress; stress plays no role in the modern analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: a few nouns mark plural LL > LH together with final-vowel shortening (Table 11); phonetic falling HL only on word-final long syllables, never on monosyllables (Table 13).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical/citation-form nouns (database of 800+ nouns elicited from four adult male Tagoi speakers in Khartoum, 2012-2022; Goy/Tagoi proper variety west of Rashad). Older group-level remark (Tucker & Bryan 1966 < Stevenson): 'Stress would also seem to have some importance, but has not been fully investigated' -- no placement given. Schadeberg & Elias 1979 (Orig dialect) likewise mark only tone (H/L) and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Bashir 2025 describes Tagoi proper (Goy; ŋo-goi), spoken west of Rashad town, from speakers resident in Khartoum. Schadeberg & Elias 1979 describe the Orig (Turjuk, ŋóórig) dialect of the same language (tago1246; Glottolog lists Orig as a Tagoi dialect). Tutschek 1848/1850 describes Tumale (Umale), another Tagoi dialect. Tucker & Bryan 1966 / Stevenson 1956-57 treat the whole Tegali-Tagoi (Rashad) group together, i.e. including Tegali/Tagom (tega1236), which is a separate Glottolog language.

sources.locator: sec. 4 'Tone on Tagoi nouns', pp. 48-49 (with sec. 1.2, p. 43)
sources.note: Sec. 1.2 p. 43 and sec. 4 'Tone on Tagoi nouns' pp. 48-50: reviews Stevenson's claim that stress (not tone) plays a marked role in Tagoi/Rashad; presents H vs L minimal pairs on mono- and disyllabic nouns and concludes the evidence favours tone rather than stress ('it might be that Stevenson noticed the pitch distinction but he attributed it to stress'); both morae of long vowels carry the same tone, no phonemic contours. No statement of where stress falls; stress is not used in the analysis.

sources.citation: Schadeberg, Thilo C. & Philip Elias. 1979. A Description of the Orig Language (Southern Kordofan), based on the notes of Fr. Carlo Muratori. (Archief voor Antropologie 26.) Tervuren: Musee Royal de l'Afrique Centrale. 85 pp. archive.org item 085-orig.
sources.note: Orig (Turjuk) dialect of Tagoi. Ch. 1 'Sounds' pp. 14-16: Muratori's four tone levels reduced to H/L; all H/L combinations occur on 1-3-syllable words; falling tones rare (word-final). Nothing at all on stress or accent (full-text grep: 'stress' only in 'we have to stress that').

sources.citation: Tutschek, Lorenz. 1850. On the Tumali alphabet. Proceedings of the Philological Society 4: 138-139 (complement to Tutschek 1848, On the Tumali language, PPS 3: 239-254). archive.org proceedingsphil11britgoog / proceedingsphil08britgoog.
sources.note: Tumale dialect, 1840s. p. 139: ultra-short 'half-vowels' each form a syllable and 'any one of which may take an accent, just like a full-toned vowel'; near-minimal sets differ by which half-vowel is accented; 'total absence of rhythm'. No rule for where the accent falls. The 1848 grammar sketch (PPS 3) has nothing on accent (alphabet section was omitted there).
